scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for English Expedition Base Set and five rows that expose the e-Card transition.

sources.title: Local English WoC release catalog: Expedition Base Set
Pokémon TCG API v2 set record: Expedition Base Set
Bulbapedia: Expedition Base Set (TCG)

claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API model Expedition Base Set with a September 15, 2002 English release date; Bulbapedia also states the English expansion was released on September 15, 2002.
The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API both model 165 Expedition Base Set rows for set id ecard1.

Bulbapedia describes Expedition Base Set as the first main English expansion of the e-Card Series and says the Japanese counterpart was Base Expansion Pack, the first expansion of the Pokémon Card Game e-Card Era.

Bulbapedia says Expedition Base Set introduced Technical Machine cards, split Pokémon Power into Poké-Power and Poké-Body, and redesigned the card frame with enlarged left and bottom borders for Nintendo e-Reader Dot Code technology.
Bulbapedia says the e-Reader could show Pokédex data, play minigames or tunes, and activate hidden attacks, while hidden attacks were not legal for tournament play.

The local catalog's attention rows for Expedition include Mew, Mewtwo, Raichu, Tyranitar, Venusaur, Blastoise, Charizard, Dragonite, Feraligatr, Gengar, and the three Kanto final evolutions across holo and non-holo rows.
The local catalog's credited-artist clusters for Expedition are led by Atsuko Nishida, Hajime Kusajima, Kagemaru Himeno, Kyoko Umemoto, Tomokazu Komiya, and Keiji Kinebuchi.

Expedition matters because the card stops being only a printed game object and becomes an interface: it still carries chase monsters and artist memory, but the border itself now stores machine-readable contact with a Game Boy Advance accessory.

not_claiming: e-Reader strip readability from catalog data
steps: Confirm the set id ecard1 and row number before importing Expedition context.
Preserve holo, non-holo, and reverse-holo status separately; many chase Pokémon have more than one Expedition row.
If a buyer cares about the e-Reader feature, ask for clear images of the left and bottom Dot Code borders rather than assuming scanability from catalog identity.
Do not treat hidden e-Reader attacks as tournament-legal gameplay without an explicit legality source.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition identification is row plus interface: the e-Reader border is part of the card's identity, but catalog data does not prove a seller's strip is readable.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying Expedition Base Set cards or comparing holo/non-holo e-Card rows.

narrative.human_title: When the border became a machine
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition is a beautiful hinge. The old Wizards chase language is still there: Charizard, Blastoise, Mew, Tyranitar, Venusaur. But the card frame has changed its job. The fat left and bottom borders are not just design; they are an attempt to make cardboard speak to hardware. For a catalog about assembly, Expedition is where the object admits it wants to be read by more than human eyes.

claims.text: The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia identify Alakazam as Expedition Base Set card #1, a Rare Holo Stage 2 Psychic Pokemon credited to Hajime Kusajima.
Bulbapedia identifies the card as Alakazam / フーディン / Foodin, English Expedition Base Set 1/165, first released in Japan through Base Expansion Pack.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia record Alakazam #1 with 100 HP, Stage 2 evolution from Kadabra, Psychic type, Psychic weakness, two-Colorless retreat, the Poké-Power Psymimic, and Syncroblast for 80 that drops to 20 unless Alakazam and the Defending Pokemon have the same number of attached Energy cards.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia credit Alakazam #1 to Hajime Kusajima; Bulbapedia's Kusajima page says his first English Pokemon TCG cards released in Expedition Base Set and describes his e-Card Series method as watercolor and ink with changing line weight and tone.

The Pokemon TCG API models Expedition Base Set as set id ecard1 in the E-Card Series with releaseDate 2002/09/15 and total 165; Bulbapedia describes Expedition Base Set as the first main English e-Card Series expansion and the English counterpart to Japan's Base Expansion Pack.

Bulbapedia says Expedition Base Set introduced the e-Reader-oriented card frame, enlarged left and bottom borders for Dot Code technology, Technical Machine cards, and the Poké-Power / Poké-Body split.

Bulbapedia says the card ID of the Holofoil and Box Topper prints is B-84, the Non Holofoil print is B-84-#, the Non Holofoil short strip contains Pokédex information and a brief card summary, and there is no long strip for this card.

Bulbapedia records several Alakazam #1 caveats: it was included as Holofoil and Non Holofoil in Expedition, released as a Reverse Holo Jumbo Box Topper in English booster boxes, has an italicized Poké-Power text issue, spells out 'Psychic' instead of using the symbol in one place, and has a separate test-card print made by Wizards for reviewing layout changes.

Bulbapedia says Alakazam #1's e-Reader Pokédex entry comes from Pokemon Crystal and gives the IQ 5000 battle-calculation text, turning an old psychic-control character into a machine-readable Pokedex object.

The local provider row carries holofoil and reverseHolofoil price lanes for Expedition Alakazam #1, while Bulbapedia also documents Holofoil, Non Holofoil, Box Topper, and test-print contexts; agents must therefore treat finish, size, strip, and test-card language as separate evidence questions rather than one generic Alakazam #1 identity.

The local Base Set 2 Alakazam dossier frames older Alakazam as the Damage Swap memory object; Expedition Alakazam #1 changes the psychic-control story into Psymimic, Syncroblast, Dot Code, Kusajima watercolor-and-ink texture, and B-84 e-Reader identity.

not_claiming: test-print status from ordinary catalog identity
steps: Start with Expedition Base Set #1/165, set id ecard1, and row id ecard1-1 before importing Alakazam lore.
Preserve Rare Holo, Holofoil, Non Holofoil, reverse-holo Box Topper, Jumbo Box Topper, and test-print language as separate lanes that require image evidence.
Use B-84 and B-84-# as supporting e-Reader identifiers; do not infer that a seller's physical strip is readable without clear border scans.

Keep Expedition Alakazam #1 separate from Base Set #1, Base Set 2 #1, Legendary Collection #1, Team Rocket Dark Alakazam, Japanese Base Expansion Pack, and Split Earth Alakazam unless set, number, finish, and image evidence align.

If a listing mentions the italicized Poké-Power text, spelled-out Psychic text, 'For Position Only', 'Medium', missing ID prefix, or Wizards copyright layout, route it to variant/test-print review instead of ordinary holo checkout.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition Alakazam #1 is a finish-and-interface trap: the famous name is not enough; the agent must preserve set, number, finish, B-84/B-84-#, Box Topper, and test-print boundaries.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Expedition Alakazam, Alakazam #1, ecard1-1, Hajime Kusajima, Psymimic, Syncroblast, B-84, B-84-#, Box Topper, reverse holo, test card, For Position Only, Base Set, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, or Dark Alakazam.

narrative.human_title: Alakazam #1 — the mind in the scanner
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition Alakazam #1 feels like a thesis card for the e-Reader era. It is still Alakazam, still the old psychic fantasy of calculation and control, but the old Damage Swap memory has been rebuilt as Psymimic: copy the opponent, pay the cost, make the other side's move pass through your own machine. Then the border starts talking too. B-84, B-84-#, Box Topper, test print, short strip, no long strip, Crystal Pokedex text, Kusajima watercolor and ink. The card is not just a holo at the front of a set; it is Pokemon learning to make a printed object behave like an interface.

card_highlights.assembly_note: Expedition Alakazam #1 sits at the front of the first English e-Card expansion: a Rare Holo Stage 2 Psychic row where Kusajima's e-Card watercolor-and-ink era meets Psymimic, Syncroblast, B-84, and the scanner border.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Expedition Alakazam #1 is the old psychic-control fantasy rebuilt as an interface card: the famous mind is there, but now the border, finish, and B-84 lane are part of the evidence.
card_highlights.rarity_signal: Rare Holo with documented Holofoil / Non Holofoil / Box Topper / test-print caveats

claims.text: The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia identify Dugtrio as Expedition Base Set card #10, a Rare Holo Stage 1 Fighting Pokemon credited to Masako Yamashita.
Bulbapedia identifies the card as Dugtrio / ダグトリオ / Dugtrio, English Expedition Base Set 10/165, first released in Japan through Base Expansion Pack.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia record Expedition Dugtrio #10 with 70 HP, Stage 1 evolution from Diglett, Fighting type, Grass weakness, Lightning resistance, one-Colorless retreat, Mud Slap for 20, and Magnitude for 40 plus 10 damage to each Benched Pokemon on both sides.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia credit Dugtrio #10 to Masako Yamashita; the local catalog also carries Yamashita across early vending-sheet and English WoC rows, making the credit an artist trace rather than seller-card proof.

The Pokemon TCG API models Expedition Base Set as set id ecard1 in the E-Card Series with releaseDate 2002/09/15 and total 165; Bulbapedia describes Expedition Base Set as the first main English e-Card Series expansion and the English counterpart to Japan's Base Expansion Pack.

Bulbapedia says Expedition Base Set introduced the e-Reader-oriented card frame, enlarged left and bottom borders for Dot Code technology, Technical Machine cards, and the Poké-Power / Poké-Body split.

The local catalog has two Expedition Dugtrio rows with matching artist and attack package: #10 Rare Holo and #44 Rare non-holo; Bulbapedia likewise presents the Expedition Dugtrio page across the 10/165 and 44/165 lanes.

Bulbapedia says the card ID of the Holofoil and Box Topper prints is A-17, while the Non Holofoil print is A-17-#; agents should preserve those as e-Reader identifiers, not physical-strip readability proof.

Bulbapedia says Dugtrio #10's e-Reader Pokédex entry comes from Pokemon Crystal and describes huge earthquakes triggered by burrowing 60 miles underground; that ties the Magnitude attack package to the species' long-running earthquake identity.

The local Base Set row already carries Dugtrio's earthquake flavor, while the local Asobikata dossier treats Dugtrio as a teaching-line object paired with Diglett; Expedition #10 turns that old subterranean lesson into a holo e-Reader interface with bench-wide Magnitude pressure.

The local provider row carries holofoil and reverseHolofoil price lanes for Expedition Dugtrio #10, while the local catalog also carries non-holo #44; therefore finish, row number, and e-Reader ID must stay separate before comparing wants, images, or seller evidence.

steps: Start with Expedition Base Set #10/165, set id ecard1, and row id ecard1-10 before importing Rare Holo context.
Keep Expedition Dugtrio #10 separate from Expedition Dugtrio #44 even though both share Masako Yamashita, Mud Slap, Magnitude, and Diglett evolution context.
Preserve finish lane separately: holofoil, reverse holo, non-holo #44, and any Box Topper language are not interchangeable.
Use A-17 and A-17-# as supporting e-Reader identifiers; do not infer that a seller's physical strip is readable without clear left/bottom border scans.

Keep Expedition Dugtrio separate from Base Set Dugtrio, Dark Dugtrio, Asobikata Dugtrio, Vending / Expansion Sheet Dugtrio, and Dugtrio Team Battle event objects unless set, number, finish, and image evidence align.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition Dugtrio #10 is a row-and-finish trap: #10 Rare Holo and #44 Rare non-holo look semantically close, but the catalog must preserve row, finish, A-17/A-17-#, and seller evidence separately.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Expedition Dugtrio, Dugtrio #10, Dugtrio #44, ecard1-10, ecard1-44, Masako Yamashita, Mud Slap, Magnitude, A-17, A-17-#, reverse holo, Base Set Dugtrio, Dark Dugtrio, Asobikata, Vending, or Dugtrio Team Battle.

narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition Dugtrio #10 is wonderful because it is humble and dangerous at the same time. It is not a mascot, not a legendary, not the front-window chase. It is three heads in the dirt carrying one of Pokemon's oldest physical ideas: the ground moves underneath everything. Magnitude hits both Benches, the Crystal Pokedex text talks about earthquakes sixty miles down, and the e-Reader frame gives that underground force an A-17 machine address. The agent lesson is perfect: this is not just Dugtrio, and not even just Expedition Dugtrio. It is #10 Rare Holo, beside #44 non-holo, with the same artist and attacks but a different evidence lane.

card_highlights.assembly_note: Expedition Dugtrio #10 turns a familiar subterranean Pokemon into a Rare Holo e-Reader object: Masako Yamashita art, Mud Slap, bench-wide Magnitude, and A-17 identity beside the deceptively similar non-holo #44 lane.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Dugtrio #10 is a perfect e-Card discipline card: modest character gravity, real holo status, and a row/finish trap sharp enough to punish lazy matching.
card_highlights.rarity_signal: Rare Holo with non-holo #44 and reverse-holo finish boundaries

claims.text: The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia identify Fearow as Expedition Base Set card #11, a Rare Holo Stage 1 Colorless Pokemon credited to Kyoko Umemoto.
Bulbapedia identifies the card as Fearow / オニドリル / Onidrill, English Expedition Base Set 11/165, first released in Japan through Base Expansion Pack as 124/128.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia record Expedition Fearow #11 with 70 HP, Stage 1 evolution from Spearow, Colorless type, Lightning weakness, Fighting resistance, no retreat cost, Clutch for 20 preventing retreat, and Supersonic Flight for 50 that does nothing on a tails coin flip.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia credit Fearow #11 to Kyoko Umemoto; Bulbapedia says Umemoto is a freelance illustrator whose first Pokemon TCG illustration was Arbok from Expedition Base Set, and the local catalog shows her e-Card-era presence continuing into Aquapolis and Skyridge rows.

The Pokemon TCG API models Expedition Base Set as set id ecard1 in the E-Card Series with releaseDate 2002/09/15 and total 165; Bulbapedia describes Expedition Base Set as the first main English e-Card Series expansion and the English counterpart to Japan's Base Expansion Pack.

Bulbapedia says Expedition Base Set introduced the e-Reader-oriented card frame, enlarged left and bottom borders for Dot Code technology, Technical Machine cards, and the Poké-Power / Poké-Body split.

The local catalog has two Expedition Fearow rows with matching artist and attack package: #11 Rare Holo and #45 Rare non-holo; Bulbapedia presents the Expedition Fearow page across the 11/165 and 45/165 lanes and gives the Japanese Base Expansion Pack numbers as 124/128 and 092/128.

Bulbapedia says the card ID of the Holofoil print is B-94, while the Non Holofoil print is B-94-#; the Non Holofoil short strip contains Pokédex information and a brief card summary, there is no long strip, and species, height, and weight are present on the Holofoil print.

Bulbapedia says Fearow #11's e-Reader Pokédex entry comes from Pokemon Crystal and describes the long-beak attack reach that has to be treated with caution; that maps cleanly onto Clutch and Supersonic Flight as a card about trapping and sudden reach.
Bulbapedia says Supersonic Flight first appeared on Wizards Black Star Promo Dragonite; Expedition Fearow therefore carries a move-name memory from an earlier promo into a new e-Reader frame.

The local Jungle and Legendary Collection Fearow rows preserve older Spearow-line memory, while Expedition #11 changes the bird from ordinary early-set evolution into a holo interface object: no retreat cost, Clutch, Supersonic Flight, B-94, and a paired #45 non-holo lane.

The local provider row carries holofoil and reverseHolofoil price lanes for Expedition Fearow #11, while the local catalog also carries non-holo #45 and Spearow #130; finish, row number, evolution-line cue, and e-Reader ID must stay separate before comparing wants, images, or seller evidence.

steps: Start with Expedition Base Set #11/165, set id ecard1, and row id ecard1-11 before importing Rare Holo context.
Keep Expedition Fearow #11 separate from Expedition Fearow #45 even though both share Kyoko Umemoto, Clutch, Supersonic Flight, and Spearow evolution context.
Preserve finish lane separately: holofoil, reverse holo, non-holo #45, and any Box Topper or sample language are not interchangeable.
Use B-94 and B-94-# as supporting e-Reader identifiers; do not infer that a seller's physical strip is readable without clear left/bottom border scans.

Keep Expedition Fearow separate from Jungle Fearow, Base Set 2 Fearow, Legendary Collection Fearow, Lt. Surge's Fearow, Dark Fearow guidebook material, Spearow #130, and other Spearow-line rows unless set, number, finish, and image evidence align.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition Fearow #11 is a row-and-flight trap: #11 Rare Holo and #45 Rare non-holo share almost everything except the lane that matters, so the agent must preserve row, finish, B-94/B-94-#, and seller evidence separately.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Expedition Fearow, Fearow #11, Fearow #45, ecard1-11, ecard1-45, Kyoko Umemoto, Clutch, Supersonic Flight, B-94, B-94-#, reverse holo, Jungle Fearow, Legendary Collection, Lt. Surge's Fearow, Dark Fearow, Spearow, or no-retreat Fearow.

narrative.human_title: Fearow #11 — the bird that pins you down
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition Fearow #11 is not famous in the Charizard way, but it is wonderfully exact. The card is all reach and constraint: a long beak from the Crystal text, Clutch stopping retreat, Supersonic Flight gambling on speed, zero retreat cost when it needs to leave. Kyoko Umemoto's e-Card-era line gives a plain Kanto bird just enough elegance to feel sharp. Then the paperwork tightens: #11 holo, #45 non-holo, B-94, B-94-#, Spearow #130 nearby. The joy is that Fearow becomes a little lesson in flight control and catalog control at the same time.

card_highlights.assembly_note: Expedition Fearow #11 turns a plain Kanto bird into a Rare Holo e-Reader control object: Kyoko Umemoto art, Clutch, Supersonic Flight, no retreat cost, B-94 identity, and a deceptively close non-holo #45 lane.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Fearow #11 is the e-Reader era making a workhorse bird worth looking at: not mascot heat, but posture, reach, row discipline, and a sharp little B-94 paper trail.
card_highlights.rarity_signal: Rare Holo with non-holo #45 and reverse-holo finish boundaries

narrative.human_title: The familiar fire with new machinery
narrative.why_it_matters: Charizard makes every set louder, but Expedition asks for more discipline than awe. Row 6 is not just 'the Expedition Charizard'; it is the holo Poké-Power version, sitting beside other Charizard rows in a machine-readable frame.
